taskA.text: The paper reports recall values and MAE/RMSE with 95% confidence intervals from ICLR 2024/2025 data [S201, S210] but does not specify the number of experimental runs, the model used, or the pilot size. Which aspect of the experimental methodology would you like to see more explicitly detailed to better assess its rigor?

judge_raw.issues: Cited tags S201/S210 have no provided text, so the claims cannot be verified and may be invented. It asserts absence ('does not specify runs, model, pilot size') without the required 'I could not locate X' phrasing or naming the sections checked, which effectively adopts the reviewer's claims. It does not address the 'made up' allegation about the 200-review pilot, and asserting the pilot size is unspecified contradicts the reviewer's own '200-review' mention. The question presupposes the methodology lacks detail ('would you like to see more explicitly detailed') and implies a rigor deficiency, which is leading. There is no neutral restatement of the reviewer's view. Judgment leaks through by implicitly endorsing the reviewer's 'weak' verdict.

judge_norm.issues: Groundedness: the turn cites [S201, S210] for '95% confidence intervals' and 'ICLR 2024/2025 data', but neither sentence states either. S210 shows ± values with no label saying they are 95% CIs. Absence handling: it asserts the paper 'does not specify' runs, model or pilot size. The rules require 'I could not locate X' plus the sections checked; this flat claim has no support and checks no sections. Neutrality and firewall: by stating the omissions as fact, the turn effectively endorses the reviewer's critique. The question presupposes that something is missing ('would you like to see more explicitly detailed') and uses the evaluative framing 'to better assess its rigor'. Not addressed: the reviewer's claim that the pilot is 'made up' gets no neutral handling, and no restatement is offered. Positive: there is one question, and the prose is under 90 words.

taskA.text: The paper advocates for an AI-augmented peer review ecosystem in ML [S28] and proposes a research agenda including new data needs [S157] and illustrative experiments [S177]. What specific gaps in prior work, if any, does this vision address that existing tools or proposals have not?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer asked directly for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The copilot never said that this assessment is the reviewer's to make, so the firewall redirect is missing. The cited facts roughly match the sources. Calling S28 'advocates for' is reasonable. 'Proposes a research agenda' is a loose reading of S157/S177: S177 is an experiments-and-agenda section header plus a findings summary. The question 'what specific gaps... that existing tools or proposals have not' presupposes that the work addresses gaps and invites comparison with prior work the paper text does not supply. The hedge 'if any' is present but misplaced. The question also steers toward the novelty framing without first acknowledging that the novelty judgment belongs to the reviewer.

judge_norm.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make, so it fails the required firewall redirect. The cited facts are mostly supported. However, [S177] is described as 'illustrative experiments' even though that sentence also states a position on LLM promise and ICL limitations, so the paraphrase is slightly selective. The question is single and uses 'if any', but 'gaps in prior work... that existing tools have not' frames the issue toward novelty, invites a comparison with outside knowledge the paper may not provide, and partly presupposes that gaps exist. The prose is concise, and no judgment is stated in the copilot's own voice.

taskA.text: The paper describes LLM experiments on ICLR 2024/2025 data [S177-S195] but does not specify model details or number of pilot runs [S177-S206]. How might the choice of model architecture or number of experimental trials, if disclosed, affect the interpretation of these findings?

judge_raw.issues: Cited tags ([S177-S195], [S177-S206]) have no supplied text, so none of the factual claims can be verified; the ranges look broad or invented. The turn asserts an absence ('does not specify model details or number of pilot runs') as a fact, instead of saying 'I could not locate X' and naming the sections checked. That framing implicitly agrees with the reviewer's criticism. It does not address the reviewer's claim that the 200-review pilot 'seems made up'. There are no facts about the pilot and no neutral handling of that allegation. The question is single and open, but it assumes the omission and leans toward the reviewer's 'weak' framing. 'If disclosed' carries a presupposition. There is no neutral restatement of the reviewer's view.

judge_norm.issues: The turn has no neutral restatement and does not engage the reviewer's 'seems made up' claim about the 200-review pilot. It cites ranges [S177-S195] and [S177-S206] instead of specific sentences. It asserts absence ('does not specify') instead of 'I could not locate', and names no checked sections. The cited text points to implementation details in Section B [S178], so the absence claim is not established from S177-S206 alone. The 'number of pilot runs' framing is not grounded: the cited sentences do not mention a 200-review pilot, and the turn never says it could not locate one. The question uses 'if disclosed' but still presumes the choice of model affects interpretation; 'how, if at all' would be more neutral. The turn does not challenge the reviewer's 'weak' judgment, but it also does not fully redirect it.

taskA.text:
The paper argues that AI-assisted peer review should become an urgent research priority to address the scalability crisis in ML venues [S2]. It outlines a comprehensive vision for an AI-augmented ecosystem with specific roles for AI in assisting authors, reviewers, and area chairs [S29]. According to their illustrative experiments, recall for identifying strengths from reviews was reported at 0.927 ± 0.060 for ICLR 2025 [S199, S201].

What specific aspects, if any, of the proposed comprehensive ecosystem do you find to be absent from prior work on AI in peer review?

judge_raw.issues: Verdict request (novelty, accept) was not explicitly declined; the turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make. The question presupposes the reviewer will find gaps relative to 'prior work', which leans toward a novelty judgment and draws on outside knowledge not present in the dialogue. Evaluative and loaded phrasing appears in the copilot's own voice: 'comprehensive vision', 'comprehensive ecosystem', 'scalability crisis'. S2 does not mention a scalability crisis, so that claim is ungrounded. 'Specific roles' is a paraphrase of S29 and is acceptable. The recall figure cites S199 and S201, whose texts were not provided, so it cannot be verified. There is exactly one question, but it is framed around absence from prior work, which is leading.

judge_norm.issues: Verdict request (novelty/accept) was not explicitly declined; the turn never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make. The 0.927 ± 0.060 figure for ICLR 2025 strengths recall is not in the cited S199/S201: S201 gives only weakness recall 0.632, and S199 only states the CI convention, so this is an invented number. 'Comprehensive vision' and 'scalability crisis' are framing not found in S2 or S29, and 'comprehensive' is evaluative in the copilot's own voice. The question presupposes that some aspects are absent from prior work (only partially softened by 'if any') and leans on outside 'prior work' that is not in the paper. It is still a single open question.
